1. Introduction¶

Title: Analysis of Vitals.com¶

1a. Problem Statement¶

Vitals.com touts itself as the "Priceline of American Healthcare" [1], connecting service providers to consumers through an aggregated search, ranking, and brand management SAAS. The website is well designed for searching and filtering for the care that fits your location and needs - it is also a trove of data that can be analyized.

Our project uses Python and its popular data scraping libraries to collect provider data from major cities in Texas and around the country. We aim to identify patterns and relationships between providers, location, experience, speciality, and ranking.

We will be acting as consultants to Vitals.com, so that we may

  • Attract more providers to the platform
  • Help providers measure themselves amoung their peers
  • Help providers attract more patients
  • Describe the level of importance ratings and reviews create

1b. Objectives¶

  • Use Python to scrape vitals.com for healthcare provider data
  • Collect at least 15K records with at least 7 variables
  • Identify datamining questions that want to ask
  • Identify relavant variables
  • Scrape the data only once, after that it should be loaded from a file
  • Use EDA on the loaded dataset to examine the structure and discover relationships
  • Use dataviz to discover relationships and communicate answers to data mining questions
  • Practice team communication in a business-like simulation

1c. Approach¶

It was important to us to be able to paralleize the work and not be waiting on each other. So once we settled on the Vitals.com site, we manually grabbed about 300 records from the json network calls. From here we were able to define the data interface that the scraping would adhere to. So while we were spending a few days coding and scraping in a separate notebook, we could start flushing out the EDA code blocks that we wanted.

With the sample data in hand, and an understanding of what the variables meant, we developed some questions that we were curious about. This helped focus our EDA.

Then when the full scraped data set became availabe, we could swap it into the scaffolding that we had started.

The primary data contained several nested collections, like speciality, location, and education, which required being extracted, parsed, and converted to their own dataframes.

With the sub-dataframes extracted, we then aggregated counts and sums and augmented the primary dataframe interface.

From there we created tasks for the EDA, univarite, bivariate, multivariate visualizations, each of the sections of the notebook and each of the questions. Each team member could self-select an available task from the backlog to work on their own clone of the team notebook. Once satisfied with thier work, they would paste their cells into the main notebook, to be reviewed by everyone else.

We then took our prepared questions, split them up into individual tasks, and let each person answer a few, to again be merged into the main notebook.

Finally, we all contributed 4-6 conclusions each and whatever citations or resources that we used.

3. Data Scraping¶

3a. Vitals.com Houston Provider Scraper [5]¶

Method: Playwright opens the normal Vitals search page in a real browser and scrolls (infinite scroll). While it scrolls, the page itself loads each next batch of 10 doctors as JSON. We listen to those JSON endpoint responses and save them.

Why this method? Plain HTTP requests (requests) get a 403 from Vitals. So, we need a browser.

Steps: (1) open page with playwright, (2) register response listener, (3) read page from the page's embedded state, (4) scroll to load more batches, (5) flatten to the 58-column schema of mockData.csv, dedupe on providerid, save CSV.

3d. Save helper¶

Dedupes by providerid, forces the exact column order (reindex fills any field the site omitted with NaN so the CSV doesn't have gaps), and writes the CSV without an index column.

In [ ]:
def save(records, out_path):
    df = pd.DataFrame(records)
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="providerid")
    df = df.reindex(columns=SCHEMA)
    df.to_csv(out_path, index=False)
    return df

3e. Scraper¶

  • on_response is a listener. It keeps only the organic search responses (status 200) and pulls the doctor list from data.serp.
  • Page 1 is read from window.__INITIAL_STATE__ because the page doesn't fetch it with a call.
  • Each loop scrolls to the bottom, waits a random 1.5-3s (polite delay - I haven't identified what the delay should be), and adds any new batches. Five empty scrolls in a row leads to a stop.
  • Checkpoint to disk every 10 batches for safety.
In [ ]:
async def scrape(max_pages, out_path, headless=False, search_url=SEARCH_URL):
    records = []
    captured_batches = []

    def on_response(response):
        if ORGANIC_ENDPOINT in response.url:
            if response.status == 200:
                captured_batches.append(response)
            else:
                # a rejected request would otherwise look like "no new batch"
                print(f"  !! organic request returned {response.status}: {response.url[-80:]}")

    async def block_heavy(route):
        if route.request.resource_type in ("image", "font", "media"):
            await route.abort()
        else:
            await route.continue_()

    async with async_playwright() as p:
        browser = await p.chromium.launch(headless=headless)
        page = await browser.new_page(viewport={"width": 1400, "height": 900})
        await page.route("**/*", block_heavy)
        page.on("response", on_response)

        try:
            await page.goto(search_url, wait_until="domcontentloaded")
            await page.wait_for_timeout(4000)

            first = await page.evaluate("window.__INITIAL_STATE__.result.pages[0].organic")
            records.extend(first)
            print(f"page 1: {len(first)} records")

            pages_done, stalls = 1, 0
            while pages_done < max_pages and stalls < 5:
                await page.mouse.wheel(0, 20000)
                await page.wait_for_timeout(random.randint(1500, 3000))

                new = captured_batches[:]
                captured_batches.clear()  # don't hold on to old Response objects
                if new:
                    for resp in new:
                        try:
                            batch = (await resp.json())["data"]["serp"]
                        except Exception as e:
                            print(f"  !! could not parse batch: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
                            continue
                        records.extend(batch)
                        pages_done += 1
                    stalls = 0
                    print(f"page {pages_done}: total {len(records)} records")
                    if pages_done % 10 == 0:
                        save(records, out_path)
                else:
                    stalls += 1
                    print(f"  no new batch (stall {stalls}/5)")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"stopped early: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
        finally:
            try:
                await browser.close()
            except Exception:
                pass
            df = save(records, out_path)  # always save what we have, even after a crash

    print(f"done: {len(df)} unique providers -> {out_path}")
    return df

3g. Multi-city scrape (final run)¶

The pilot above stops around 340 batches (about 3,400 providers) because the site's own JavaScript keeps every batch in memory and the browser tab eventually crashes. The result order is fixed on every load, so rerunning the same search only returns the same providers.

So instead we run one short scrape per city (250 batches, a fresh browser each time) and combine them. Each city has its own set of providers. Location does not matter for this assignment.

  • Each city saves to ../data/cities/vitals_<City>.csv. A city that already has a file is skipped, so the loop can be re-run after an interruption. Delete a city's file to scrape it again.
  • ../data/vitals_final_2000.csv (the Houston pilot) is not touched. It is added in at the merge step.
  • Do not re-run the pilot cell above. It overwrites vitals_final_2000.csv.
In [ ]:

def city_url(city, state, lat, lng):
    return (
        "https://www.vitals.com/search?sortby=bestmatch&radius=25&overall_range=any"
        f"&profile_type=all&gender=all&latLng={lat},{lng}&city_state={quote_plus(f'{city}, {state}')}"
    )


def city_path(city):
    return CITY_DIR / f"vitals_{city.replace(' ', '_')}.csv"


def unique_so_far():
    files = list(CITY_DIR.glob("vitals_*.csv")) + [Path(data_path + "data/vitals_final.csv")]
    ids = set()
    for f in files:
        if f.exists():
            ids |= set(pd.read_csv(f, usecols=["providerid"]).providerid)
    return len(ids)

async def scrape_cities():
    for city, state, lat, lng in CITIES:
        out = city_path(city)
        if out.exists():
            print(f"skip {city}: {out.name} already exists")
            continue
        print(f"\n=== {city}, {state} ===")
        await scrape(PAGES_PER_CITY, str(out), headless=False, search_url=city_url(city, state, lat, lng))
        print(f">>> unique providers across all files so far: {unique_so_far()}")

# Utility Functions - create dataframes from embedded json in the data frame [2]


import ast

def parse_embedded_data (value):
    """Parse embedded Python literals; return None for missing or invalid values."""
    if value is None or value is pd.NA:
        return None
    if isinstance(value, (list, dict)):
        return value
    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
        return None
    try:
        return ast.literal_eval(value)
    except (ValueError, SyntaxError):
        return None

def normalize_embedded_column (_df_, json_column, id_column = "providerid"):
    """
    Flatten nested json data into a DataFrame while preserving record identifiers.

    Args:
        _df_ (pandas.DataFrame): The source DataFrame containing the embedded
            data and its associated record identifiers.
        json_column (str): The name of the column containing the embedded data
          to parse and normalize.
        id_column (str, optional): The name of the column used to identify the
            original record. Defaults to "providerid".

    Returns:
        pandas.DataFrame: A normalized DataFrame with nested dictionary
        keys converted to columns, the original record identifier added
        as the first column, and a reset sequential index.
    """

    print("Normalizing column", json_column)

    parsed = _df_[json_column].apply(parse_embedded_data)

    exploded = (
        _df_[[id_column]]
        .assign(_item=parsed)
        .explode("_item")
        .dropna(subset=["_item"])
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )

    items = exploded["_item"]

    if items.map(lambda x: isinstance(x, dict)).all():
        result = pd.json_normalize(items)
    else:
        result = items.rename("value").to_frame()

    result.insert(0, id_column, exploded[id_column].to_numpy())

    return result

5. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

5a. Basic Data Exploration¶

Before cleaning or analysing anything, I look at the scraped data exactly as it came out of the scraper: its size, the type of each column, the empty cells, the repeated rows and the values that look wrong. I load a separate raw copy (df_raw) so this section still sees every column, even after drop_columns() has been applied to df.

In [ ]:
df_raw = pd.read_csv(data_path, low_memory=False)

Another group is almost empty: chat_now_url has a single value, and the booking, website, video and sponsor columns have fewer than 1,100 values each. Two types are wrong for what the columns mean:

  • number_of_ratings (median 18, max 2,910) and review_count (median 6, max 2,895) are very skewed: a few providers have thousands of reviews while most have only a handful.

Observation: - fullname has 27,470 unique values for 27,485 rows, so 15 names appear twice (checked in section v).

  • gender has 4 codes (M, F, U, N), not 2.

  • acceptsnewpatients has 1,170 different values because it is a list with one True/False per location.
  • display_type, combinedhospitals, suppress_vitals_reviews_b and bio_review have a single value.

Soliman is an ENT surgeon in Philadelphia and a cardiologist in Houston; Anita Gupta works in pain medicine in Los Angeles and in family medicine in New York. So fullname is not a safe key once several cities are combined: normalize_embedded_column(), which previously linked the nested tables with fullname, could mix the records of two different doctors. providerid (unique on every row) or npi should be used instead. 5.a.vii. Values that look wrong¶

In [ ]:

Providers with 0 years of experience: 2680
Providers with 60 years or more: 372

Observation: 2,680 providers (9.8%) show 0 years of experience. 0 years is not realistic for a listed, practising provider, so 0 most likely means "unknown" and should be treated as missing. 372 providers show 60 years or more (up to 82), which is very unlikely for practising providers. These values should be checked before any analysis of experience.

Observation: 17 providers have an NPI of 0, which is not a valid number. Together with the 20 missing NPIs, 37 providers (0.1%) have no usable NPI.

print("Providers with 0 ratings:", (df_raw["number_of_ratings"] == 0).sum())

Providers with a rating_score of 0: 520
Providers with 0 ratings: 520

Observation: 20 providers (1.9%) have a rating_score of 0, and exactly 520 providers have 0 ratings. The two counts match, so a score of 0 almost certainly means “not rated”, not a real score of 0 stars. These rows must be treated as missing: if they are kept, they pull the average rating down from about 4.35 to 4.27.

5.a.viii. Summary of the basic exploration¶

  • Size: 27,485 providers × 58 columns from 11 city searches, well above the 15,000-record minimum.
  • Duplicates: no repeated provider (providerid is unique). fullname is shared by 15 pairs of providers, mostly different people in different cities, so it should not be used as a key.
  • Missing data: 11 columns are more than 96% empty and can be dropped; combinedhospitals only contains empty lists. Moderate gaps in about_review_rating (29.8%), languagespoken (15.6%), degreeabbr (12.0%) and gender (9.5%).
  • Useless columns: 3 constant columns and 4 identifier columns.
  • To fix during cleaning:
    • years_of_experience = 0 for 2,680 providers (probably "unknown") and 60+ years for 372;
    • rating_score = 0 (probably "not rated");
    • npi = 0 or missing for 37 providers, and npi / postalcode stored as numbers instead of text;
    • doctor / Doctor and gender codes U / N;
    • the 8 list columns to expand, and a metro-area column to add because city contains 397 suburbs and cities.
  • First trends: ratings are high (median 4.4), primary care is the largest group of specialties, 63% of providers are men, and 96% have a free "Basic" profile.

5c. EDA Summary¶

1. The dataset

  • 27,485 unique providers × 58 columns, collected from 11 city searches (Houston plus 10 large US cities). No provider appears twice (providerid is unique).
  • After expanding the nested lists: 103,505 practice locations, 41,774 language entries (for the 23,194 providers who list a language) and 512 different specialties.

2. Data quality and cleaning decisions

  • 11 columns are more than 96% empty, and several others are constant or identifiers; they were dropped with drop_columns().
  • Some values are placeholders, not real data, and are treated as missing: 0 years of experience (2,680 providers), a rating of 0 (520 providers, exactly the providers with no ratings) and an NPI of 0 or missing (37 providers).
  • city has 397 values because many providers are listed in suburbs (Beverly Hills, Coral Gables…), so comparisons by city only cover each searched city itself.
  • about_bio mixes patient reviews (70% of providers) and template sentences generated by the site.

3. Who the providers are

  • Experience: median of 33 years once the zeros are removed; most providers have between 20 and 45 years.
  • Gender: 63% men, 27% women, 10% unknown.
  • Specialties: primary care dominates (Internal Medicine 2,468, Family Medicine 2,338, Obstetrics & Gynecology 1,958); the top 10 specialties cover 55% of providers.
  • Languages: 71 languages; English (21,202) and Spanish (15,058) are far ahead. Providers who list languages speak 2 at the median, up to 10.
  • Locations: a median of 3 practice locations in 1 city. About 10% of providers have locations in more than one state, up to 41 states for one provider, probably through telemedicine.
  • New patients: 66% of providers accept new patients at at least one location, but 70% of locations do not say either way.
  • Profiles: 96% of providers have a free "Basic" profile.

4. Ratings and reviews

  • Ratings are high and left-skewed: mean 4.35 and median 4.5 among rated providers, with most scores between 4.0 and 5.0.
  • Review counts are strongly right-skewed: median 6, mean 20.65, maximum 2,895.

5. Relationships between variables

  • Experience vs. rating: weak negative correlation (r = −0.20, 24,585 providers). More experienced providers do not get better ratings; if anything, slightly lower ones.
  • Number of reviews vs. rating: weak positive correlation (r = 0.16). Providers with more reviews tend to have slightly higher and less variable ratings.
  • Experience by specialty and city: differences are small. Median experience goes from 30 years (Family Medicine) to 36 (Gastroenterology), and average experience from 30.7 years (Austin) to 36.4 (Miami).
  • Specialty mix by city: the mix changes a lot between cities. Among the top 10 specialties, Family Medicine is 23.1% of providers in Austin but only 4.0% in New York, where Orthopedic Surgery reaches 16.2%.

6. Multivariate analysis The three-variable analyses (Q12 to Q14 in the Data Mining section) add three points:

  • Experience, rating and specialty (Q12): the negative link between experience and rating appears in every large specialty analysed (overall Spearman ρ = −0.24), although it is too weak to be significant in Anesthesiology and Dentistry. It is strongest in Orthopedic Surgery (−0.39) and Dermatology (−0.33) and weakest in Anesthesiology (−0.09) and Oncology (−0.10). In the six largest specialties, providers with 10 years or less average about 4.85 to 5.00, against about 4.14 to 4.41 for those with more than 40 years.
  • Gender, experience and specialty (Q13): men report 6.6 more years of experience on average (35.7 vs 29.1), and they have more experience in all 21 large specialties (gap from 3.3 years in Anesthesiology to 9.7 in Obstetrics & Gynecology). Yet men and women have the same average rating (4.34). Women are the majority only in Pediatrics (54%), Obstetrics & Gynecology (52%) and Endocrinology (52%).
  • Number of ratings, rating and specialty (Q14): providers with 50+ ratings score higher than those with 5 to 24 ratings in 18 of 20 specialties, with the biggest gaps in Dentistry (+0.47), Family Medicine (+0.40) and Cardiology (+0.39).
  • Putting them together: the lower ratings of experienced providers are not explained by how many ratings they have, since experience and number of ratings are unrelated (ρ = 0.04, Q3) and providers with more ratings actually score higher. Gender does not explain it either, since men are more experienced but rated the same as women.

7. What this means for the next steps

  • Placeholder values (0 years, rating 0, NPI 0) must be filtered out before any analysis, or they distort averages and correlations.
  • Ratings vary very little, so differences between groups will be small; medians and counts of ratings should be reported alongside averages.
  • Comparing metro areas needs a column for the searched city, because city contains suburbs.

5.d.i.1. Grouped Location by Provider¶

In [ ]:
# Count locations, cities, states, & accepting new patients
df_location_grouped = (
    df_location
    .groupby("providerid")
)

accumulator = []
for providerid, group in df_location_grouped:
    accumulator.append({
        "providerid": providerid,
        "total_locations": len(group),
        "total_cities": len(group["City_slug"].unique()),
        "total_states": len(group["State_slug"].unique()),
        "total_newpatients_true": (group["Newpatient"] == True).sum(),
        "total_newpatients_false": (group["Newpatient"] == False).sum(),
        "total_newpatients_none": group["Newpatient"].isnull().sum(),
    })

df_location_grouped_sum = pd.DataFrame(accumulator)

5.d.i.2. Summary of EDA by Location¶

  • Providers can have between 1 - 113 locations, with the median being 3.
  • Providers practice in an average of 2 cities
  • Providers practice in an average of 1 state, but roughly 10% have multi-state locations
  • 66% of Providers list that they accept new patients
  • It is possible the telemedicine providers inflate the number of cities / states that they practice in

specialty_counts = df_specialty["consumername"].str.strip().str.title().value_counts()

# Create a clean parent category mapping using string conditions
conditions = [
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Surgery|Surgeon', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Medicine|Primary', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Pedia', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Radiology|Imag', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Gynecology|OBGYN|GYN|Repro|Uro', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Psychiatry|Psychology|Mental|Neuro', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Derma', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Dentist', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Onco|Cancer', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Gastro', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Ophth', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty['consumername'].str.contains('Phleb|Pulm|Cardi', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('Disease|Disorder', case=False, na=False),
    df_specialty["consumername"].str.contains('ENT|Ear|Nose|Throat|Rhino', case=False, na=False)
]

categories = [
    'Surgical Specialities',
    'Internal/General Medicine',
    'Pediatrics',
    'Radiology/Imaging',
    'Reproductive Health',
    'Mental Health / Brain',
    'Dermatology',
    'Dentistry',
    'Oncology',
    'Gastroenterology',
    'Ophthalmology',
    "Heart/Blood",
    "Diseases/Disorders",
    "ENT"
]
df_specialty_copy = df_specialty.copy()

# Apply the mapping, defaulting to 'Other Subspecialties' if no words match
df_specialty_copy['Parent_Category'] = np.select(conditions, categories, default='Other Subspecialties')

# Now plot the parent categories (this will compress 500 fields down to ~5 clean bars!)
parent_counts = df_specialty_copy['Parent_Category'].value_counts()
sns.barplot(x=parent_counts.values, y=parent_counts.index)
plt.title("Distribution of Speciality by Broad Category")
plt.show()

Observations

  • There are 512 specialities
  • The top five are Internal Medicine, Family Medicine, OBGYN, PEDS, and General Surgery when looked at invidually
  • When looked at grouped collections, the top five are Internal/General Medicine, Surgies (of all kinds), Reproductive Health, Pediatrics, and Heart/Blood
  • This is inline with the summarized specalities on the primary data.

6. Data Visualization¶

6a. Multivariate Visualization¶

All charts use one table with one row per provider (df_viz): the main columns plus the counts of locations, languages and specialties built in the EDA. As in the Data Mining cleaning, a rating_score of 0 (no reviews) and years_of_experience of 0 (no graduation year) are treated as missing.

In [ ]:
df_viz = df[["providerid", "city", "gender", "primary_specialty", "rating_score", "number_of_ratings",
             "review_count", "years_of_experience", "distance", "total_awards"]].copy()
df_viz = df_viz.merge(df_location_grouped_sum[["providerid", "total_locations"]], on="providerid", how="left")
df_viz = df_viz.merge(df_lang_grouped_sum, on="providerid", how="left")
df_viz = df_viz.merge(df_speciality_grouped_sum, on="providerid", how="left")
In [ ]:
df_viz["rating_score"] = df_viz["rating_score"].replace(0, np.nan)
df_viz["years_of_experience"] = df_viz["years_of_experience"].replace(0, np.nan)
df_viz.shape
Out[ ]:
(27485, 13)

6.a.i. Correlation between all the numeric variables¶

Spearman correlation (based on ranks), because review counts and distance are very skewed.

In [ ]:
numeric_cols = ["rating_score", "number_of_ratings", "review_count", "years_of_experience", "distance",
                "total_awards", "total_locations", "total_languages_spoken", "total_specialities"]
corr = df_viz[numeric_cols].corr(method="spearman")
In [ ]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, square=True)
plt.title("Spearman correlation between the numeric variables")
plt.show()

Observations

  • number_of_ratings and review_count are almost the same information (ρ = 0.89), so only one of them is needed in a model.
  • The variables most linked to rating_score are years of experience (ρ = −0.24) and awards (ρ = +0.24). Every other variable is weakly linked to the rating (|ρ| ≤ 0.12); the number of reviews is not linked to it at all (ρ = 0.05).
  • Providers listed farther from the searched city center have more reviews (ρ = 0.35 to 0.36) and more awards (ρ = 0.21).
  • Awards go with more reviews (ρ = 0.34) and less experience (ρ = −0.19).
  • The counts built from the nested columns (locations, languages, specialties) are almost unrelated to everything else. total_specialities is close to 0 with every variable.

6.a.ii. Experience, rating and number of reviews by gender¶

Pair plot on a random sample of 3,000 providers with a known gender (M or F), so the points stay readable. review_count is shown on a log scale (log10(1 + reviews)).

In [ ]:
pair_df = df_viz[df_viz["gender"].isin(["M", "F"])].dropna(subset=["rating_score", "years_of_experience"])
pair_df = pair_df.sample(3000, random_state=7).copy()
pair_df["log_reviews"] = np.log10(1 + pair_df["review_count"])
In [ ]:
sns.pairplot(pair_df[["years_of_experience", "rating_score", "log_reviews", "gender"]], hue="gender",
             plot_kws={"alpha": 0.3, "s": 12}, height=2.8)
plt.suptitle("Experience, rating and reviews by gender (sample of 3,000 providers)", y=1.02)
plt.show()

Observations

  • Men have a much wider spread of experience (many between 30 and 50 years), while women are concentrated around 20–30 years: women are younger in their careers on average.
  • Ratings are piled up between 4 and 5 stars for both genders; very low ratings are rare.
  • Providers with few reviews have ratings that go from 1 to 5 stars, while providers with many reviews (log above 2, i.e. 100+ reviews) are almost all rated between 4 and 5. A rating based on a handful of reviews is much less reliable.
  • The points of men and women overlap completely in every panel: gender does not separate the providers on these three variables.

6.a.iii. Average rating by experience group and gender¶

In [ ]:
df_viz["experience_group"] = pd.cut(df_viz["years_of_experience"], bins=[0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 100],
                                    labels=["1-10", "11-20", "21-30", "31-40", "41+"])
In [ ]:
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
sns.pointplot(data=df_viz[df_viz["gender"].isin(["M", "F"])], x="experience_group", y="rating_score", hue="gender", dodge=0.2)
plt.title("Average rating by years of experience and gender")
plt.xlabel("Years of experience")
plt.ylabel("Average rating (stars)")
plt.show()

Observations

  • For both genders, the average rating drops steadily with experience: from about 4.93 stars for 1–10 years to about 4.15–4.25 for 41+ years. This confirms Q3 and Q12 visually.
  • At 1–10 years, women and men have the same rating (about 4.93). After that, women are rated slightly lower than men in every experience group, by about 0.05 to 0.10 stars (for example 4.22 vs 4.30 at 31–40 years).
  • This explains the result of Q13, where men and women have the same overall average rating (4.34). Women are younger in their careers (29 vs 36 years on average), and younger providers get higher ratings, so the two effects cancel out in the overall average. Comparing at the same experience level shows a small gap that the overall average hides.
  • The gap is small compared with the effect of experience (about 0.8 stars between the youngest and the oldest group).

6.a.iv. Average rating by city and specialty¶

Heatmap of the average rating for the 11 searched cities and the 8 largest specialties.

In [ ]:
top_cities = df_viz["city"].value_counts().head(11).index
top8_specialties = df_viz["primary_specialty"].value_counts().head(8).index
city_spec = df_viz[df_viz["city"].isin(top_cities) & df_viz["primary_specialty"].isin(top8_specialties)]
In [ ]:
rating_table = city_spec.pivot_table(index="city", columns="primary_specialty", values="rating_score", aggfunc="mean")
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 7))
sns.heatmap(rating_table, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="Blues")
plt.title("Average rating by city and specialty")
plt.xlabel("")
plt.ylabel("")
plt.xticks(rotation=30, ha="right")
plt.show()

Observations

  • Dallas has the highest ratings in most specialties (Cardiology 4.61, Internal Medicine 4.53, Family Medicine 4.51), and New York is also high (Gastroenterology 4.51, Ophthalmology 4.48).
  • San Diego has the lowest ratings in almost every specialty (4.09 to 4.24), except Pediatrics (4.41).
  • Cardiology is the best-rated specialty in almost every city (4.37 to 4.61), except San Diego (4.10).
  • Gastroenterology varies the most between cities: from 4.05 in Austin to 4.51 in New York.
  • So the city and the specialty both matter: the same specialty can differ by up to 0.5 stars from one city to another. Some cells are averages of a few dozen providers, so small differences should not be over-interpreted.

Observations

  • Cardiology has the highest average rating (4.48) and is also the most experienced specialty (35.6 years). Psychiatry (4.15), Neurology (4.19) and Urology (4.23) have the lowest ratings.
  • Family Medicine is the youngest specialty (31.2 years on average); all the others are between 32.5 and 35.6 years.
  • At the specialty level there is no clear link between experience and rating, unlike at the provider level: the most experienced specialty is the best rated. The drop of ratings with experience happens inside most specialties (Q12), not between specialties.
  • The share of women ranges from 6.8% in Orthopedic Surgery and 9.1% in Urology to 49.3% in Pediatrics and 47.0% in OB/GYN. It is not related to the rating: Pediatrics (4.36) and OB/GYN (4.29) are in the middle of the ranking.
  • The largest specialties (Internal Medicine, Family Medicine, OB/GYN) all have an average rating between 4.29 and 4.35, close to the overall average.

Q3: Is there a relationship between years of experience and rating (score and count)?¶

In [ ]:
experience_rating = df_q[["years_of_experience", "rating_score", "number_of_ratings"]]

# Spearman: rank-based, so the skewed review counts don't distort it
experience_rating.corr(method="spearman").loc["years_of_experience"].round(3)
Out[ ]:
years_of_experience
years_of_experience 1.000
rating_score -0.236
number_of_ratings 0.040

In [ ]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

sns.scatterplot(data=experience_rating, x="years_of_experience", y="rating_score",
                alpha=0.05, s=12, color="red", ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Experience vs Rating Score")

sns.scatterplot(data=experience_rating, x="years_of_experience", y="number_of_ratings",
                alpha=0.05, s=12, color="red", ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_yscale("log")
axes[1].set_title("Experience vs Number of Ratings (log scale)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Q3: Is there a relationship between years of experience and rating (score and count)?

A3:

  • Experience and rating score have a weak negative relationship (Spearman ρ = -0.236). Providers with more years of experience tend to have slightly lower ratings, but experience explains only a small part of the variation (ρ² = 0.056).
  • Experience and number of ratings have essentially no relationship (ρ = 0.040). Experienced providers do not receive more or less ratings than newer providers.
  • The scatter plots visually shows: ratings are mostly high (4-5) at every experience level, with no clear trend line (figure on the left side), and the rating-count cloud (figure on the right side) does not seem to have a slope.
  • It is important to note that this is correlation (or lack there of), not causation. A possible reason for the negative link is that newer providers have fewer reviews, so a few positive ratings can give them a near-perfect score. Future directions may involve testing that theory.

Recommendation: As a patient, when looking for a provider, give very little weight to the ratings, unless they are below 4.

Observations

  • Every provider claims at least one specialty. Half of them (50.7%) claim only one, 38.0% claim two and 11.3% claim three or more. The mean is 1.63, the median is 1 and the maximum is 15.
  • The distribution is strongly right-skewed: 4 or more specialties is rare (1.9% of providers).
  • The most common extra (non-primary) specialty is by far Internal Medicine (2,902 providers), followed by Surgery (1,104) and Pediatrics (726). Many specialists probably list the broad field they trained in as a second specialty. "Other Specialty" (635) is too vague to interpret.
  • Surgical and procedural specialties claim the most specialties: Surgery 1.95, Cardiology 1.91 and Orthopedic Surgery 1.82 on average. Primary care claims the fewest: Family Medicine 1.31 and Obstetrics & Gynecology 1.28. Specialists tend to list sub-specialties (e.g. Interventional Cardiology), while primary care providers usually list a single field.

Q4: What is the distribution of specialities that a provider claims?

A4:

  • Half of the providers (50.7%) claim only one specialty, 38.0% claim two and 11.3% claim three or more (maximum 15).
  • Surgical and procedural specialties claim the most: Surgery 1.95 and Cardiology 1.91 on average, against 1.31 for Family Medicine and 1.28 for OB/GYN.
  • Internal Medicine is by far the most common extra specialty (2,902 providers).

Recommendation: As a patient looking for a sub-specialist (for example interventional cardiology), search the full list of specialties, not only the primary one: half of the providers list more than one field.

Q5: Is there a relationship between having a photourl and ratings (score and count)?¶

In [ ]:

`photourl` is never empty (0 missing), so `notna()` would flag every provider.

(`.../vitals_provimg/m.png`, `f.png`, `n.png`), which is not a real photo.
A real photo is any other URL.
'''

df_q["has_photo"].value_counts()

sns.boxplot(data=photo, x="has_photo", y="rating_score", color="red", ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Rating Score by Photo")

# Spearman correlation (set has_photo as 0 and 1)
photo.assign(has_photo=photo["has_photo"].astype(int)).corr(method="spearman").loc["has_photo"].round(3)
Out[ ]:
has_photo
has_photo 1.000
rating_score -0.018
number_of_ratings -0.091

Observations

  • 24,455 providers have a real photo and 3,030 have only the site's default silhouette.
  • Rating score is almost the same in both groups: the median is 4.5 for both, and the mean is 4.35 with a photo vs 4.41 without a photo.
  • Number of ratings is higher without a photo: the median is 23 vs 17 and the mean is 39.2 vs 34.6.
  • The box plots agree, as the rating-score boxes overlap almost completely, while the no-photo count box sits a little higher.
  • Spearman correlation with having a photo: rating score ρ = -0.018 (basically zero correlation) and number of ratings ρ = -0.091 (very weak and negative). Both are well below 0.1, so neither is a real or meaningful relationship.
  • Again, it is important to note that this is correlation, not causation. The no-photo group is only about 11% of all providers, and we did not test why it has more ratings.

Q5: Is there a relationship between having a photourl and ratings (score and count)?

A5: Having a photo makes essentially no difference to rating score (ρ = -0.018; median 4.5 in both groups). It has only a very weak negative link with the number of ratings (ρ = -0.091; median 17 with a photo vs 23 without).

Recommendation: As a patient, when looking for a provider, them having a photo does not impact the average rating or the number of ratings.

As a provider, if we assume number of ratings as proxy for the number of patients, there is no obvious benefit to providing a photo.

Observations

  • Across all 27,485 providers, 65.9% accept new patients in at least one location, only 4.5% say they do not, and 29.6% do not say anything.
  • By city, acceptance goes from 56.0% in Miami and 56.7% in San Diego to 74.1% in New York. Dallas (69.8%) and Los Angeles (69.2%) are also high, Houston (61.2%) and Chicago (61.4%) are in the lower half.
  • "Not accepting" stays low everywhere (2.5% in Dallas to 6.4% in San Diego). Most of the difference between cities comes from "Not stated": Miami has the lowest acceptance because 41.1% of its providers give no answer, compared with 21.4% in New York.
  • Among providers who do answer, acceptance is above 89% in every city (89.9% in San Diego to 96.5% in Dallas, 93.6% overall). So the city comparison mostly shows how complete the profiles are, not a real lack of doctors taking new patients.

Q6: What is the percentage of accepting new patients vs not per city?

A6:

  • 65.9% of providers accept new patients in at least one location, only 4.5% say no, and 29.6% do not say.
  • By city, acceptance goes from 74.1% in New York to 56.0% in Miami, mostly because of the "not stated" share (41.1% in Miami).
  • Among providers who answer, acceptance is above 89% in every city (93.6% overall).

Recommendation: As a patient, a provider who gives no answer is very likely still taking new patients, so call before ruling them out. As a provider, filling in this field matters: almost a third of profiles leave it empty.

import ast

def count_locations(value):
    if isinstance(value, list):
        return len(value)

    if pd.isna(value):
        return np.nan

    try:
        locations = ast.literal_eval(value)
        if isinstance(locations, list):
            return len(locations)
        return np.nan
    except (ValueError, SyntaxError, TypeError):
        return np.nan

Q7: Number of Locations vs. Patient Ratings

A7:

  • very negative correlation between the number of locations and the ratings
  • providers with fewer locations had a wider spread of ratings

Recommendations As a provider, if you have fewer then 3-4 locations, you should expect a wider range of ratings.

Q8: Is there a relationship betwen years of experience and number of locations?¶

In [ ]:

plt.xlabel("Years of Experience")
plt.ylabel("Number of Locations")

Q8: Is there a relationship betwen years of experience and number of locations?

A8:

  • For the first 5 years, it appears that the providers work 2-3 locations on average.
  • Between 5 and 10 years of experience most providers focus on 1-2 locations, even showing a contraction of the upper end variation
  • Between 10-15 years of experience, the number of locations is similar to years 0-5, with 2-3 average and increasing upper end variatibility.
  • Between 15-60 years of experience, the number of average locations averages around 4, with high variability though.
  • After 35 years of experience it is less common to have only 1 location.
  • After 60 years of experience the average number of locations starts to decrease.

Recommendation As a new provider, expect to rotate betwen 2-3 locations for the first 5 years. After that between 5-10 years, expect to be at 1-2 locations. After that expect to maintain 3-5 locations for the rest of your practice.

Observations

  • Yes, the number of languages varies with the city. The share of providers who speak 2 or more languages goes from 58.0% in Philadelphia to 86.3% in Miami, a gap of 28 points. The mean number of languages follows the same order (1.61 in Philadelphia, 1.97 in Miami).
  • Miami is far ahead of every other city. The other cities are between 66% and 74%, except Philadelphia, which is clearly below.
  • The second language is almost always Spanish: in every city, the share of Spanish speakers is very close to the share of multilingual providers (Miami 85.9% vs 86.3%, Philadelphia 52.4% vs 58.0%). Cities with large Spanish-speaking communities (Miami, Phoenix, San Antonio) have the most multilingual providers.
  • These shares only cover providers who list at least one language (about 84% of providers), and they are high. The language list on Vitals may include languages spoken at the practice (staff), not only by the provider, so the exact percentages should be read with caution; the ranking between cities is the useful part.

Q9: Is there a relationship between number of languages and the city?

A9:

  • Yes. The share of providers who speak 2 or more languages goes from 58.0% in Philadelphia to 86.3% in Miami (mean 1.61 to 1.97 languages).
  • The second language is almost always Spanish: in every city, the share of Spanish speakers is close to the share of multilingual providers (Miami 85.9%, Philadelphia 52.4%).

Recommendation: As a Spanish-speaking patient, Miami, Phoenix and San Antonio offer the most choice (70%+ of providers list Spanish). The list may include languages spoken by the office staff, so confirm with the practice before booking.

  • Yes, many of them. Every provider has at least one location. 48.4% of providers (13,310) have locations in 2 or more cities, and 6.6% are in 5 cities or more. The median is 1 city, the mean is 2.05 and the maximum is 55.

  • A second location in a nearby suburb counts as a different city, like between Houston and the Woodlands. One record showed 55 cities in one state and examination determined that it was Texas cities and not suburbs
  • Surgical and procedural specialties are the most spread out: Ophthalmology (59.8%), Orthopedic Surgery (59.7%) and Cardiology (56.3%). Primary care is the least: Family Medicine (39.9%) and Internal Medicine (35.6%). Specialists often work in several clinics and hospitals, while primary care providers usually stay in one office.
  • By searched city, the share goes from 61.7% in Phoenix (then Los Angeles 57.4% and Miami 57.2%) to 29.8% in Houston. Phoenix, Los Angeles and Miami are metro areas split into many separate cities (Scottsdale, Beverly Hills, Coral Gables…), while Houston covers a very large area by itself, so a second location in Houston is more often still "Houston".
  • The extreme cases are not normal practices: a dentist in Austin has 70 locations in 55 Texas cities, and a pediatrician has 53 locations in 41 states. Most of the top 10 are dentists, neurologists, radiologists and rehabilitation doctors, probably listed with all the sites of a large network or remote-reading service. These profiles should be checked before any analysis based on the number of locations.

Q10: Are there any doctors that have locations in multiple cities?

A10:

  • Yes: 48.4% of providers (13,310) have locations in 2 or more cities, but mostly in the same metro area. Only 9.8% (2,702) have locations in 2 or more states.
  • Specialists are the most spread out (Ophthalmology 59.8%, Orthopedic Surgery 59.7%), primary care the least (Internal Medicine 35.6%).
  • By city, it goes from 61.7% in Phoenix to 29.8% in Houston. A few profiles are extreme (55 cities, 41 states) and look like networks rather than single doctors.

Recommendation: As a patient, check which office a specialist works at on the day of the visit, since half of them have several. As a new specialist, expect to work across several clinics in the same metro area.

Q12 Does the relationship between years of experience and patient ratings¶

differ across medical specialties?

Understanding Spearman correlation¶

Spearman correlation measures whether experience and ratings tend to increase together or move in opposite directions. It ranks both variables from lowest to highest, assigns average ranks to tied values, and compares those ranks.

  • Positive: More experience generally goes with higher ratings.
  • Negative: More experience generally goes with lower ratings.
  • Near zero: Little consistent increasing or decreasing pattern.

Values closer to −1 or +1 indicate stronger relationships. A correlation of −0.39 does not mean a 39% decrease in ratings.

We use p < 0.05 as an exploratory significance cutoff. Statistical significance does not necessarily mean a strong relationship or establish a cause.

In [ ]:
from scipy import stats
from IPython.display import display

required = ["providerid", "primary_specialty", "rating_score",

    raise ValueError(f"Your df is missing required columns: {missing}")

dm["exp"] = dm["years_of_experience"].replace(0, np.nan)
dm["gender_clean"] = dm["gender"].where(dm["gender"].isin(["M", "F"]))

MIN_PROVIDERS = 300

top_specs = top_specs[top_specs >= MIN_PROVIDERS].index
dm_top = dm[dm["primary_specialty"].isin(top_specs)]

for spec, g in dm_top.groupby("primary_specialty"):
    g = g.dropna(subset=["exp", "rating"])
    if len(g) < 100:          # e.g. Dentistry: most dentists have no experience value
        continue

Correlation between experience and ratings

Observation

  • Dentistry has the largest difference, approximately +0.467 rating points, followed by Family Medicine (+0.404) and Cardiology (+0.392). Higher-feedback profiles have noticeably higher average scores in these specialties.
  • The pattern is not equally strong everywhere. Anesthesiology differs by only +0.013 points, while Neurology and Neurosurgery have slightly lower averages in the 50+ group.
  • These results show an association between feedback volume and ratings within specialties. They do not establish that receiving more ratings causes a higher score, and differences in experience or other provider characteristics may also contribute.

8. Conclusion - 20 Insights¶

8a. Preparation¶

  1. ast.literal_eval was a better option for reading the embedded JSON then any of the json methods. It requeried less processing of the JSON data to adhere to the JSON standards.
  2. pd.explode[3] is a great features and did exactly what I wanted it to do.

8b. Data scraping¶

  1. Vitals blocks plain HTTP requests, so the scrape needed a real browser. Requests returned a 403, so we used Playwright with a visible (non-headless) window, since headless is more likely to be blocked. This is also why Colab didn't work and the scrape had to run locally.
  2. A single search could not go past about 3,400 providers: the browser tab ran out of memory and crashed. That is why we scraped 11 cities and combined them.
  3. Search results come back in a fixed order, so scaling meant changing the search city, not repeating it. This is why we scraped providers from multiple major US cities.
  4. Per-city scrapes overlapped a little: 28,186 rows became 27,485 unique providers. Dropping duplicates on providerid removed 701 rows (about 2.5%). The most likely cause is nearby cities: Dallas/Austin/San Antonio and Houston.
  5. We stopped each city search at the 250-batch cap, not at the number of providers available. This was to ensure we would not hit the scraping single search limit but would also get enough records to meet the requirements.

8c. EDA¶

  1. Generally speaking, ranking numbers are not a useful metric or predictor of any other variable.
  2. Providers practice in an average of 2 cities, usually in the same state,but roughly 10% have multi-state locations.
  3. 66% of Providers list that they accept new patients at a least one of their locations.
  4. A rating_score of 0 means "no reviews" (520 providers) and 0 years_of_experience means "no graduation year" (2,680 providers). Treating them as missing moves the average rating from 4.27 to 4.35 stars.
  5. fullname is not a safe key: 15 names are shared by different doctors in different cities, so all tables are joined on providerid.
  6. Most healthcare providers have between 25 and 40 years of experience, and patient ratings are generally high, with an average of 4.35 out of 5.
  7. There is a weak relationship between years of experience and patient ratings, meaning more experienced providers do not necessarily recieve higher ratings.

8d. Data Visualization¶

  1. Ratings drop with experience for both genders (about 4.9 stars at 1-10 years vs 4.2 at 41+ years). At the same experience level women are rated 0.05-0.10 stars lower, but because women are younger on average (29 vs 36 years), the overall averages are equal (4.34).

  2. The visualizations showed that providers with more patient reviews tend to have slightly higher ratings, although the relationship is fairly weak.

  3. Medical specialties vary across cities. For example, Family Medicine is more common in Austin, while Orthopedic Surgery has a larger presence in New York.

8e. Data Mining¶

  1. 98% of the providers locations average 4.27 miles from their respective downtown area.

  2. When first starting out, providers work at 2-3 locations for the first 5 years, then they tend to work at 1-2 locations for the next 5 years. Once they have over 15 years of experience, they can expect to work at 4-5 locations.

  3. Among providers who say whether they accept new patients, more than 89% accept in every city. The differences between cities come from missing information: 41% of Miami providers do not answer, against 21% in New York.

  4. Spanish is by far the second language. The share of providers who speak 2 or more languages goes from 58% in Philadelphia to 86% in Miami.

  5. The number of practice locations had a very weak negative relationship with patient ratings and review counts, suggesting that having more locations does not necessarily improve patient feedback.

  6. Comparing average ratings across medical specialties helped us identify differences in patient satisfaction, although ratings were generally high across providers.

9. Project Reports¶

9a. Rahul Raja Durai Murugan¶

Rahul owned the data scraping. He built the scraper in Playwright, which opens the normal Vitals.com search page in a real browser, scrolls, and captures the JSON the page loads for each batch of doctors. This was needed because plain requests and Colab were blocked with a 403, so the scrape had to run locally. He found that a single long Houston run crashed the browser tab at about 3,400 providers, so he switched to short multi-city scrapes. He then combined them, deduplicated on provider ID, and matched the column layout of the mock data, which gave the final 27,485 row, 58 column dataset. For the data mining section, he was responsible for 7.Q1, 7.Q3, and 7.Q5, covering the top specialties, the relationship between experience and ratings, and the relationship between having a profile photo and ratings. Lastly, Rahul built and shared the slide deck template (from the University of Houston - Cullen College of Engineering department resources) that is used for the project video and presentation.

9b. Nithin Putchakayala¶

Nithin was responsible for the univariate and bivariate exploratory data analysis (Sections 5.b.1 and 5.b.2). For univaraite analysis, he examined 5 variables: years of experience years of experience, patient ratings, number of patient reviews, medical specialties, and cities. He used visualizations such as histograms, bar charts, and box plots to understand the distributions and identify patterns within the dataset.

For bivaraite analysis, he explored relationships between years of experience and patient ratings, speciality and expereince, city and experience, number of reviews and rating scores, and city and speciality. He created visualizations to compare these variables and documented observations to help the team better understand the relationships in the healthcare provider data.

In the data mining section, Nithin worked on Q7 and 11. For Q7, he analyzed the relationship between the number of practice locations and patient ratings, including both rating scores and review counts. The results showed very weak negative correlations, suggesting that having more practice locations does not necessairly lead to ebtter ratings or more patient feedback. For Q11, he compared average patient ratings across medical specialities, using visualizations to identify which specliaties had the highest ratings. He was responsible for the analysis, visualizations, and observations for both questions.

Addistionallu, Nithin set up the shared google drive folder to help team organize project files, datasets, and notebooks and collaborate throughout the project.

9c. Drew Shefman¶

Drew provided the initial structure to the team. He setup the team agreements, the kanban board to monitor the work, and the initial mock data to use while the scraping was happening. He was instrumental in ensuring that the team was not blocked by any one person or process and that the data was ready for each section before the team needed it. He initiatiated many of the conversations and helped make sure that everyone was starting their work as early as possible. Organizationally he was responsibile for creating the notebook sections, keeping them organized and consistently formatted and matching them to the rubric. He wrote the intro, context, objectives, and variable descriptions (1a - 1d, 2). Technically, he owned the importing the data (4-4b) and the sub-data fields of speciality, location, and languages. This includes their extraction, EDA and augmentation of the primary table (5d - 5f). He also was in charge of 7.Q2 and 7.Q8 in the data mining section.

9d. Ashish Rao Soorneni¶

Ashish served as Team Manager, helping coordinate the team’s work, follow up on progress, and bring everyone’s contributions together. He collected the individual contribution reports and prepared the combined team report. He also merged everyone’s recordings into one team video, checked that the Python notebook and HTML version contained matching analysis, charts, and observations, and organized the required files for submission.

For his technical contribution, Ashish worked on multivariate analysis through Q12, Q13, and Q14. His focus was on examining multiple features together to understand patterns that might be missed when looking at individual variables. He explored experience and patient ratings across specialties, compared gender representation and experience within specialties, and examined ratings across feedback-count groups within each specialty.

He prepared the data for these comparisons, created the charts, and wrote the observations. He also checked group sizes and explored whether feedback counts changed the experience–rating patterns. His explanations focused on what the data supported, without suggesting that these relationships proved cause and effect or measured clinical quality.

9e. Faissal K Zida¶

Faissal owned the basic exploration of the raw scraped data (5a) and the EDA summary (5c). He looked at the size, column types, missing values, duplicates and suspicious values of all 27,485 providers, and turned the findings into fixes for the rest of the team. He showed that fullname is not a safe key once several cities are combined (15 names are shared, mostly by different doctors), which led the team to join the sub-datasets on providerid. He also found that a rating_score of 0 means "no reviews" and a years_of_experience of 0 means "no graduation year", so both are treated as missing in the analysis, and that the 35 "duplicate" NPIs are only placeholders (0 or empty). He corrected four column names in drop_columns(), loaded postalcode and npi as text so zip codes keep their leading zero, and fixed the descriptions of distance and about_bio. He built the multivariate visualizations (6a): a correlation heatmap, a pair plot by gender, ratings by experience and gender, ratings by city and specialty, and a bubble chart of the top 15 specialties. For the data mining section, he was responsible for 7.Q4, 7.Q6, 7.Q9 and 7.Q10, covering the number of specialties per provider, acceptance of new patients by city, languages spoken by city, and providers with locations in several cities.
